transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. I, um... I hope I'm in the right place, and not just wasting your time. 

I'm here because... well, it feels a little embarrassing to admit. I know it probably sounds incredibly vain for a woman my age, but I just can't seem to stop fixating on my face. Specifically, there's this awful droop and unevenness right around my mouth and my jawline. 

I see it in every single mirror, every photo... even when people tell me I look perfectly fine. I know they're just trying to be nice, but the asymmetry is just so glaringly obvious to me. It's actually—and I feel terrible admitting this—but it's gotten to the point where I've started avoiding my clients. I'm an architect, so I usually have to do a lot of presentations, but I've been making excuses to get out of them because I just can't stand the thought of people staring at my face. 

I'm sorry, I know I shouldn't let something like this get to me so much. Does that make sense? I just feel a bit silly even talking about it out loud.
Have you noticed any changes in how your face moves or feels, like weakness or numbness, that might explain the asymmetry you're seeing?

No, no, nothing like that. I haven't noticed any weakness or numbness or anything medical like that. I feel perfectly fine physically, I promise. It's just... it's just the way it looks. I know it sounds like I'm making a mountain out of a molehill, and I really hope I'm not coming across as dramatic. It's just that I see this sagging and this crookedness so clearly. But physically, my face moves just fine. Is that what you meant? I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

Can you describe what you see when you look at your face? Is it something that you believe has changed over time, like signs of aging, or do you feel like it looks abnormal compared to how a typical person's face should look?

Well, like I mentioned a moment ago—and I'm sorry if I'm repeating myself, I just want to make sure I'm being clear—it's mostly that droop and the unevenness around my jawline. I know at fifty-four, I should expect some wrinkles and changes, and I really try to tell myself it's just normal aging. I don't want to seem like someone who just can't accept getting older. But... um... it just looks completely abnormal to me. Not like a typical face at all. 

When I look in the mirror, or if I see a photo, it's just so lopsided. And like I said, people tell me I look fine, and I always just smile and thank them because I don't want to make a fuss or seem ungrateful, but... it's just so glaringly obvious to me. It's why I've been hiding from my clients and backing out of my architecture presentations. I just can't bear the thought of them staring at how abnormal my mouth looks while I'm trying to speak. I know I shouldn't let it affect my job like that, and I feel really guilty about it. Am I making sense? I hope I'm answering your question the right way.
When you look at your face, does it feel like the issue is about aging or general appearance, or does it feel more like a specific defect that you can’t stop thinking about?

I know I keep bringing up the same things, and I'm so sorry if I'm talking in circles. But to answer your question... it definitely feels more like a specific... well, "defect" sounds so dramatic, and I really try not to be an obsessive person. But yes, it's that one specific thing. 

It doesn't feel like just general aging to me. It's exactly what I was saying before—I just can't stop fixating on that exact droop and the unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It's in every single reflection and photo. And even though people tell me I look fine, and I try so hard to believe them, it just feels so obvious to me. 

It's the whole reason I'm here, honestly. I just can't stop thinking about it, and it's why I've started avoiding my presentations and my clients. I feel so ashamed letting this one specific issue take over my life like this. Did that answer what you were asking? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.
If someone confirmed that the asymmetry you see was actually there and visible to others, would that make you feel better, or would you still be just as distressed about it?

Oh... um... that's a really good question. I guess... well, on one hand, if someone finally just admitted they saw it, maybe I wouldn't feel quite so... oh, I don't know, like I'm losing my mind? I hate feeling like I'm making things up when everyone tells me I look fine. 

But... honestly? I think I would still be just as distressed. Probably even more so. Because then I'd know for an absolute fact that my clients and colleagues really are staring at this crookedness when I'm trying to present my designs. 

I'm so sorry, I know that sounds incredibly vain. I really, really don't want to come across as some superficial person who only cares about her looks, especially at my age. I know I should be past all this, and I try so hard to just be a professional. I just... I think it would still upset me terribly to know everyone sees it. Is that an okay answer? I want to make sure I'm giving you the right perspective on all this.

If a specialist, like a dermatologist or plastic surgeon, told you that your face is completely normal and that there's no visible asymmetry, would that relieve your worry, or would you still feel the same way?

Well... um... I know I probably should say that a doctor telling me it's normal would make me feel better. And I really, really wish it would. I don't want to be difficult or seem like I don't trust medical professionals, because I do. I respect doctors so much. 

But... if I'm being completely honest—and I hope it's okay to admit this—I think I would still feel exactly the same. I've actually had people, you know, friends and family, tell me I look fine, just like I mentioned before. And I always smile and agree with them because I don't want to make them uncomfortable. But inside... it doesn't change anything for me. 

Because... well, like I said, I'm here because I just can't stop seeing that droop and the unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It's there in every single reflection, every photo. It's just so overwhelmingly obvious to me, no matter what anyone else says. And it's gotten to the point where I'm avoiding my clients and backing out of my architecture presentations because of it. 

I feel so terrible admitting that a specialist wouldn't be able to talk me out of it. It makes me sound so stubborn, doesn't it? I really try to be reasonable, I promise. But the worry is just... it's just always there. Does that make sense? I hope I'm not coming across as too irrational.

latest_inference.note: The patient's persistent preoccupation with a perceived defect in her facial appearance, despite reassurance from others and absence of any identifiable medical cause, strongly supports the diagnosis of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD). The patient acknowledges that even confirmation from a specialist that there is no visible asymmetry would not relieve her distress, which is a key feature of F45.22 (Body Dysmorphic Disorder). F40.00 (Agoraphobia) is ruled out as the avoidance is specifically tied to perceived facial defect rather than fear of places or situations.
